title: AI Inference and its Privacy and Confidentiality Challenges
thesis: Most AI inference today gives users no privacy or confidentiality guarantee, but running the whole serving stack inside hardware trusted execution environments with remote attestation already works in production at low single-digit GPU overhead, so there is no excuse not to offer it.
summary: Romailler frames confidentiality as the neglected leg of the CIA triad for AI and compares today's state to the era before end-to-end encrypted messaging. He argues most providers offer no guarantees while people confide medical, psychological and work material to chatbots, and cites two examples: OpenAI's statement that it cannot rule out de-identified usage data improving its models in the dispute with an NYU mathematician, and a 22.7 TB aggregator breach exposing chat logs and corporate documents. He then walks through a typical inference pipeline (load balancers, API gateway, inference router, prefill and decode nodes, secret weight shards) and a messier real one with multiple routers and providers where nothing is verifiably private. He lists inference threats: prompt and response privacy, harvest-now-decrypt-later, targeted serving of custom responses to a specific user (non-targetability), weight leakage, and trojanized models. He asks where to draw the trust boundary. His answer is TEEs (trusted execution environments) and confidential VMs with remote attestation rooted in hardware manufacturers, with the trust boundary drawn around Kubernetes rather than including it. A table of NVIDIA Blackwell GPU overheads (about 2 percent, under 1 percent, about 1.5 percent on four GPUs, 10 to 13 percent for training) supports the cost claim.
argument: Confidentiality of user prompts and responses matters and is not guaranteed by most AI providers, as shown by the aggregator breach and the training-data uncertainty.
Real inference pipelines span gateways, routers and multiple providers, so TLS hops alone give no end-to-end privacy assurance.
Inference faces additional threats beyond privacy: quantum harvest-now-decrypt-later, targeted custom responses, weight theft and trojanized models.
Where the trust boundary sits depends on the threat model (user data versus weights), so teams must choose it explicitly.
TEEs and confidential VMs with remote attestation let the whole inference stack, including the router and gateway, sit inside the boundary without trusting Kubernetes or cloud operators.
Measured overhead for confidential GPU inference is small, so cost and complexity are not valid reasons to withhold private inference.

claims.claim: Most AI providers do not come with any privacy or confidentiality guarantees for user data.
claims.evidence: Stated on a slide; a few notable exceptions were mentioned but not named.

claims.claim: OpenAI said it cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from product usage may have helped improve its models, in connection with a Navier-Stokes proof dispute with an NYU mathematician.
claims.evidence: A New York Times headline and an OpenAI statement shown on a slide; the speaker explicitly said no causal link to missing confidentiality is established.

claims.claim: The 302.ai aggregator breach exposed 22.7 terabytes through an unsecured database, including chat logs, prompts, AI responses and confidential corporate documents.
claims.evidence: Slide text and a news screenshot dated October 22, 2026 referring to over 18 million files; the speaker said 22 terabytes.

claims.claim: A model can be steered to serve a specific user custom responses, and the user would most likely not notice; this non-targetability threat is hard to solve and complicates billing.
claims.evidence: Reasoned argument; the slide cites 26 percent of users ending their browsing session after reading an AI summary (sample size 900 individuals) and says steering a model to be evil is easy.

claims.claim: Confidential virtual machines give hardware isolation and encrypted memory, so sysadmins and cloud providers cannot read data during processing; the residual trust is in hardware vendors such as AMD, Intel and NVIDIA.
claims.evidence: Conceptual explanation with a slide listing TEE technologies (Intel SGX deprecated, Arm TrustZone, Apple Secure Enclave, Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, Nvidia CC).

claims.claim: Remote attestation is the keystone: a hardware-manufacturer-rooted trust chain and challenge-response show the TEE is running the expected software through launch measurements and report data.
claims.evidence: Explained on slides without a demo.

claims.claim: Confidential Kubernetes lets the TEE boundary wrap the gateway, router and nodes so Kubernetes control plane is outside the trust boundary, and many companies have run this in production for months.
claims.evidence: Trust-boundary diagrams comparing standard and confidential Kubernetes; the production claim is asserted without named companies.

claims.claim: Single-GPU confidential-computing overhead is about 2 percent with the overlap scheduler off and under 1 percent with full CUDA graphs plus CC patches.
claims.evidence: Table citing Asad and Grunseid, arXiv 2608.26575 (benchmarking confidential computing on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs) and an NVIDIA blog with similar single-digit results.

claims.claim: Mixture-of-experts serving on four GPUs (TP4) costs about 1.5 percent overhead from prefill all-reduce over encrypted NVLink, scaling roughly linearly with GPU count (about 3 percent on eight GPUs).
claims.evidence: Table row for 4 GPUs; the eight-GPU inference figure is an extrapolation stated aloud, not a measured table row.

claims.claim: Training is much costlier in confidential mode, at roughly 10 to 13 percent on eight GPUs, a hardware floor, but training need not run in a TEE.
claims.evidence: Table row citing encrypted NVLink collectives.

claims.claim: Trust-and-safety monitoring is still possible inside an enclave by baking in auditable observability, such as a classifier running inside the TEE, and TEEs can verify each other through attestation.
claims.evidence: Q&A answer with no implementation shown.

claims.claim: Meta's confidential computing for Muse is probably not yet running in a TEE, and users should verify attestations; Apple Private Cloud Compute already uses TEEs.
claims.evidence: Q&A opinion; the speaker said not to trust that it currently runs in a TEE and to verify.

claims.claim: Every big tech company has a confidential computing team, so confidential computing is here to stay.
claims.evidence: Q&A assertion naming OpenAI, Intel, NVIDIA and others, without sources.

frameworks.name: Inference pipeline model
frameworks.description: Client, L4 and L7 load balancers around an API gateway, inference router with KV-cache tracker map, prefill nodes, decode nodes sharing KV cache, and secret weight shards; split into network-based routing and token-aware routing.

frameworks.name: Inference threat list
frameworks.description: Prompt and response privacy, harvest-now-decrypt-later (quantum), targeted attacks serving a specific user custom responses, proprietary model weight leaks, trojanized models.

frameworks.name: Where do you draw the line
frameworks.description: Trust boundary choice: at the load balancer, after it excluding the inference router, or only around weights and inference; each reflects a different threat model.

frameworks.name: TEE mechanics
frameworks.description: Hardware isolation, dedicated core per enclave, random secret key in a register encrypting memory, remote attestation via launch measurements, report data and append-only registers; some add a dedicated coprocessor and underclocked core against side channels.

frameworks.name: Confidential Kubernetes trust boundary
frameworks.description: A TEE boundary enclosing load balancers, API gateway, router and GPU nodes, leaving the Kubernetes control plane outside it.

slide_only: Slide wording on the NYT item: 'An N.Y.U. Mathematician Clashed With OpenAI Over a $1 Million Proof' (Tristan Buckmaster) and the OpenAI statement that no specific user data or Codex sessions were accessed but it cannot rule out de-identified usage data improving its models over time.

The aggregator breach slide names 302.ai and a news headline 'Security breach at AI aggregator exposes over 18 million files, including some very embarrassing chat records', published October 22, 2026.

Real-world pipeline diagram shows users reaching an AI Router, an Other Router and a Third Router (with router-to-router links) which fan out to three separate AI providers each with its own gateway, router, nodes and secret weight shards.

Unusual-threat slide: AIs are permeating society and taking decisions on our behalf; abliteration is not always for good reasons; steering a model to be evil is easy; 26 percent of users end browsing after an AI summary (sample 900).

Table 'Where the cost comes from / Recoverable?': one GPU overlap scheduler off is residual per-sync setup and near floor; full CUDA graphs plus CC patches is per-step cost removed and at floor; MoE four GPUs is prefill all-reduce over encrypted NVLink, not recoverable but O(number of GPUs); eight-GPU training is encrypted NVLink collectives, hardware floor. Footer: confidential computing on Blackwell costs little when the stack is configured for it and a lot when it is not.

Takeaways slide: TEEs are the de facto standard for confidentiality in AI inference; the threat model can feel paranoid and the attack surface daunting but is manageable; be concerned about the data you share with AI as most setups cannot ensure privacy.

quotes.text: There is no excuse nowadays not to provide private confidential inference.
quotes.speaker: Yolan Romailler

quotes.text: Non-targetability is a new issue we are not too used to dealing with when it comes to cyber security, and yet it is a very concerning threat when it comes to AI inference.
quotes.speaker: Yolan Romailler

quotes.text: If you don't have any attestations, be careful about what's going on here.
quotes.speaker: Yolan Romailler

offense: Targeted serving: routing a specific user to a customized or steered model to shape their opinions, undetectable to the user.
Harvest now, decrypt later against traffic protected by non-quantum-safe mechanisms, including some TEE-related technology.
Weight theft by a cloud sysadmin or competitor on shared infrastructure, for resale.
Trojanized open models served by arbitrary providers behind routers.
Data exposure through misconfigured aggregator databases holding prompts, responses and corporate documents.
Intermediate operators (gateways, multiple routers and providers) seeing plaintext prompts and responses since there is no end-to-end guarantee.
defense: Run the inference stack, including gateway and router, inside confidential VMs with GPU confidential-computing mode and keep Kubernetes outside the trust boundary.
Require remote attestation (launch measurements and report data) and verify it before sending data, including having clients or an LLM verify the attestation.
Use the attested report data to deliver a public key and establish a secure channel to the enclave.
Make everything inside the enclave auditable by outside reviewers, and keep safety classifiers and metrics inside the TEE rather than abandoning observability.
Pick the trust boundary deliberately by threat model: user data, router, or weights only.
Treat claims of confidential computing from providers as unverified until attestations can be checked.
takeaways: Assume prompts sent to a provider without verifiable attestation are readable by operators and possibly retained; classify what you send accordingly.
When buying or building inference, ask for remote attestation evidence and published launch measurements, not just a policy statement.

Do not accept performance as a reason to skip confidential inference: published Blackwell numbers show roughly 1 to 3 percent overhead for inference with a configured stack, though training is 10 to 13 percent.
Draw and document the trust boundary for each AI workload separately for user data versus model weights; keep orchestration such as Kubernetes outside it.
Add non-targetability and trojanized-model risk to AI threat models, especially when using routers or aggregators.
limits: TEE threat modeling is daunting with many extra moving pieces, and some TEE technology is not yet quantum safe.
Trust still rests on hardware vendors not having backdoors.
Training in confidential mode carries a 10 to 13 percent overhead hardware floor, which is why training is excluded.
Non-targetability is hard to solve, needing oblivious HTTP style sessions that complicate billing.
Some TEE overhead only reaches the low figures when the stack is configured for it; it is large when it is not.
critique: The performance table rests on a single cited benchmark paper (and a vendor blog) on Blackwell hardware; the talk gives no own measurements, model sizes, batch sizes or latency tail results, and the eight-GPU inference figure is an extrapolation.

The speaker works for a company that sells confidential AI inference; the remaining costs (attestation operations, side-channel attacks on TEEs, key management, supply of enclave-ready stacks) were not addressed in detail.

Known TEE attack classes (side channels, physical and firmware attacks, attestation bugs) were mentioned only through the phrase 'paranoid threat model', and the talk did not present evidence on whether today's technology withstands them.
The 'many companies in production' claim names no deployments except Apple in Q&A, and the claim about Meta not yet running in a TEE is opinion.

Non-targetability is raised as a headline new threat, yet the talk names no concrete mitigation inside the TEE design beyond oblivious HTTP, and the connection of the 26 percent AI-summary statistic to the threat was not explained.
The OpenAI example is explicitly not tied to a confidentiality failure, so it is evidence of uncertainty rather than harm.
qa: Q (audience, on antivirus leaking data as an inconsistency, then asked): How do you run a trust and safety department at a provider without looking at what users do? A: Bake observability into the enclave, let auditors review source for no exfiltration path, and run a classifier inside the TEE for safety features; TEEs can also attest to each other.

Q: Are you encouraged that Meta announced confidential computing for Muse? A: Yes, he is excited by any adoption; Meta reportedly collaborated with Moxie Marlinspike, but he does not believe the current version runs in a TEE, so verify; Apple Private Cloud Compute uses TEEs and attestations should be verified.

Q: Opaque Systems (organizer of the Confidential Computing Summit) was reportedly acquired by an AI lab; is that encouraging? A: Every big tech company has a confidential computing team; the community must create demand and refuse to surrender chat confidentiality.

key_frames.caption: Real-world inference topology: users reach multiple routers that fan out to several AI providers, each with its own gateway, router, nodes and secret weight shards, so no hop is verifiably private.
List of inference threats: prompt and response privacy, harvest-now-decrypt-later, targeted custom responses, weight leaks and trojanized models.
Trust boundaries diagram: confidential Kubernetes draws the TEE boundary around gateway, router and nodes while the control plane stays outside.
Confidential inference overhead table with the cited Blackwell paper: about 2 percent, under 1 percent, about 1.5 percent on four GPUs, and 10 to 13 percent for eight-GPU training.
TEE overview: hardware isolation, memory encryption key and remote attestation via launch measurements, report data and append-only registers.

signal.reason: The talk presents TEE-based confidential inference with an overhead table drawn from one cited benchmark and does not cover attacks on TEEs in detail.

caveats: Auto-caption garbles: speaker's name appears as Yolan Romayer; the slide spells Romailler. Moxie Marlinspike appears as Maxi Marlinspike.

In the Q&A an audience member said an organizer of the Confidential Computing Summit was acquired by a lab the captions render as 'Entropic'; the acquirer and the organizer name are not confirmed on any slide and are not recorded as fact. The first question's opening remark was partly garbled.

The transcript says 22 terabytes and 'users and sex dolls' as a joke about the breach contents; the slide says 22.7 terabytes and lists chat logs, prompts, responses and confidential corporate documents.
The speaker's 8 GPU inference overhead (about 3 percent) was spoken as an extrapolation and is not in the table.
Arxiv ID 2608.26575 and the version date are legible only in small footer text on the slide.
No live demos; the recording after the contact slide shows only Q&A camera shots with no slide content.
